title: The Sunk Cost Trap
objective: After this level you can explain why money or time already spent should not decide what you do next.
summary: A sunk cost is already spent whichever way you choose, so only what lies ahead should decide. Its pull is strong, and it often rests on an unstated premise.

cards.headline: You paid for the concert. It's pouring and you have a cold. Go anyway?
cards.body: Plenty of people would drag themselves out, so the money isn't "wasted". But look closely: the money is gone whether you go or not. This level is about why that matters for every choice you make next.

cards.headline: Spent is spent
cards.body: A sunk cost is one you can't avoid because it has already happened. An accounting textbook puts the rule bluntly: a sunk cost won't change whichever option you pick, so it has no bearing on the decision. The concert ticket is sunk. The only live question is whether tonight is better in the rain or on the sofa.

mascot.line: People mix this up: the cost was real. It just can't be a reason anymore.

cards.headline: The old car
cards.body: OpenStax's accounting textbook gives an example. Last year you spent $1,600 on car repairs. Now you must choose between repairing it again and trading it in. That $1,600 shouldn't count in the choice: it's spent whichever way you go. What counts is what each option costs and brings from here on.

cards.headline: Why it pulls so hard
cards.body: People show a greater tendency to keep going with something once money, effort or time has gone into it: the sunk cost effect. Part of the pull, the textbook notes, is that letting go means admitting a decision went wrong. Try Level 7's hidden-premise test on "I paid, so I should go." It needs "money already spent should decide what I do next". Said out loud, that wobbles.

cards.headline: Sunk costs: seen through
learned: A sunk cost has already happened and cannot be avoided
It doesn't change between options, so it can't decide
Its pull is strong, partly because quitting admits a mistake
"I paid, so I should" hides a premise worth questioning

questions.prompt: Match each idea about sunk costs with its description.

pairs.right: A greater tendency to keep going
In the rain or on the sofa

questions.explanation: A sunk cost is one you can't avoid because it has already happened. The sunk cost effect is a greater tendency to keep going once money, effort or time has gone in. The only live question is whether tonight is better in the rain or on the sofa.

questions.prompt: Sam is halfway through a dull novel and wants to stop. Which reason for finishing falls into the sunk cost trap?

options.label: The ending is said to be the best part
options.rationale: That's a future benefit, a fair reason.

options.label: A book report on it is due on Friday
options.rationale: That's a future cost of stopping, a fair reason.

options.label: I've already put hours into it
I'm starting to like the characters
options.rationale: That's future enjoyment, a fair reason.

questions.explanation: The hours are spent whether Sam finishes or not. Only what finishing would bring from now on should count.

questions.prompt: "I paid for this ticket, so I should go." Which unstated premise does it lean on?

options.label: Tickets these days are too expensive
options.rationale: True or not, price doesn't get you to "should go".

options.label: Concerts are better in good weather
options.rationale: That's a reason not to go, if anything.

options.label: The band will play this same town again next year
options.rationale: That doesn't link paying to going.

options.label: Money already spent should decide what I do next

questions.explanation: Ask what else must be true for the conclusion to follow: that past spending should steer the choice. Stated, it's the sunk cost trap.
